title: Prompt for Extraction? PAIE: Prompting Argument Interaction for Event Argument Extraction
research_question: Can prompt-based joint span extraction improve sentence- and document-level event argument extraction while handling long-range dependencies, multiple same-role arguments, limited supervision, and inference efficiency?
methodology: PAIE reformulates event argument extraction as role-conditioned span selection using BART, with the event context processed by the encoder and a joint multi-role prompt by the decoder. Role-specific representations generate start and end span selectors, while multiple prompt slots allow several arguments to share one role and bipartite matching provides permutation-invariant assignment to gold spans. The model is evaluated on ACE05, RAMS, and WIKIEVENTS using argument-identification and argument-classification F1, with additional argument-head F1 for WIKIEVENTS. The authors compare against classification, QA, and generation baselines and perform ablations, long-distance, same-role, few-shot, and inference-speed analyses.

key_findings.finding: PAIE performs direct evidence-span extraction: an argument is represented by its start and end offsets and associated with an event role.
key_findings.section: Methodology: Formulating Prompt for Extraction; Task Definition

key_findings.finding: PAIE achieved the strongest reported results in the paper on all three evaluated benchmarks, including base-model Arg-C scores of 69.8 on ACE05, 49.5 on RAMS, and 63.4 on WIKIEVENTS.
Joint multi-role prompts consistently improved performance over single-role prompting, supporting the value of modeling interactions among argument roles.
Bipartite matching contributed an average Arg-C improvement of about 0.7 percentage points across the three benchmarks.
On WIKIEVENTS roles containing three or at least four arguments, PAIE exceeded EEQA-BART by 9.5 and 26.4 Arg-C F1 points respectively.
key_findings.section: Analysis on Real Scenario: Same-role Argument Assignment

key_findings.finding: PAIE improved extraction of arguments located in sentences away from the event trigger, particularly arguments occurring after the trigger.
key_findings.section: Analysis on Real Scenario: Long-range Dependencies

key_findings.finding: In few-shot experiments, PAIE generally outperformed the QA baselines and could reach comparable performance to EEQA-BART with roughly 20% of the training data and to EEQA with roughly 10%.
key_findings.section: Analysis on Real Scenario: Few-shot Setting

key_findings.finding: PAIE was reported to run roughly three to four times faster than EEQA-style sequential role extraction because it predicts multiple roles jointly.
key_findings.section: Analysis on Real Scenario: Inference Speed

limitations: The experiments concern general event argument extraction rather than workplace email or chat action items.
The formulation assumes an event trigger and event type are already supplied, so it does not solve end-to-end task or decision detection.
The number of slots for multiple arguments of one role is heuristically set from the maximum observed in training data, which can limit extrapolation to higher unseen cardinalities.
Long documents are processed using a trigger-centered window because full contexts can exceed encoder length and memory limits.
The authors identify coreference and entity information as future work for improving argument resolution and boundaries.
The benchmarks do not specifically evaluate task owners, deadlines, conditional obligations, or negated obligations.
Although span-role binding is explicit, temporal expressions are not treated as a workplace-specific deadline relation to an action.
raw_claims: PAIE casts event argument extraction as selecting text spans for event-specific roles.
A joint prompt contains the role slots associated with one event type.
Role-specific selectors predict the start and end tokens of argument spans.
Multiple slots for one role allow more than one argument to receive the same role.
Bipartite matching is used to align multiple same-role predictions with gold arguments.
The experiments use ACE05, RAMS, and WIKIEVENTS.
Joint prompts outperform single-role templates in the reported prompt comparisons.
PAIE performs particularly strongly when one role has several arguments.
The model shows improved performance on long-distance document-level arguments.
PAIE is reported to be substantially faster at inference than sequential QA extraction.
The paper provides a public GitHub repository for the model code.
